# Memory Architectures {#sec-memory}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** One small local measurement — a contradiction
probe on `qwen3.5:9b` through `ollama` 0.24.0, short prompts, minutes to run —
plus published results where the question needs scale this book cannot supply.
The probe is greedy with one run per item, so its results are sensitive to which
thirty items were drawn; whether the same input gives the same answer across
runs (different hardware, parallelism or server version) was not tested. The
three prompt templates and the bucketing rule are not published, so the
measurement cannot be reproduced independently.
@sec-context-engineering covers what happens *within* a run; this chapter is
about what survives *between* them. Software: NumPy 2.5.2 on Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- distinguish working, episodic and semantic memory, and pick storage for each;
- define a write policy — what gets remembered, when, and who decides;
- handle staleness and contradiction instead of accumulating stale facts;
- test a memory at the write, at the read, and across many sessions;
- reason about consent and deletion in a system that remembers people.

## Three kinds of memory, three different problems {#sec-memory-kinds}

"Memory" in an agent is used for three different functions. Separating them is
the first step and most of the design work, because each has a different
lifetime, a different storage answer, and a different failure mode.

| | what it holds | lifetime | where it lives | how it fails |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Working** | the current transcript and transient state — the task, recent steps, live tool results | one run, or between two checkpoints | the context window and application state | it fills up, gets truncated or summarised. @sec-context-engineering is entirely about this |
| **Episodic** | what happened, and when: past conversations, actions taken, outcomes | across runs | a timestamped, append-only event log, with a search index where needed | it accumulates. Volume grows without bound and old episodes crowd out useful ones |
| **Semantic** | durable facts: preferences, entities, relationships, learned rules | depends on the fact and the retention policy: until contradicted, expired or deleted on request | a store you can update *and* delete from | it goes **stale** or contradicts itself, and a stale fact can do more harm than an absent one |

: One word, three problems {tbl-colwidths="[14,32,12,20,22]"}

The distinction that matters most in practice is the last column. Working
memory usually fails loudly — you hit the window and something raises. Not
always: @sec-context-engineering's whole subject is the quieter version, where
everything fits and the middle of a long context stops being used well.
Episodic memory fails slowly — the system gets more expensive and less
relevant.

[Semantic memory fails silently]{.hl}: a fact recorded in March is still
returned confidently in July, and nothing in the system knows it has expired.
That asymmetry is why most of this chapter is about semantic memory even
though it is the smallest of the three by volume.

::: {.column-margin}
The human analogy is where the vocabulary comes from and it is worth not
leaning on too hard. What matters here is engineering: episodic memory is an
event log, semantic memory is a mutable key-value store with provenance, and
the fact that people's memory blurs the two is not a reason for your system
to.
:::

You will also meet a fourth kind in the literature: **procedural memory**,
knowledge of *how* to do the task. The widely used agent taxonomy
([CoALA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02427), Sumers et al.) lists working,
episodic, semantic and procedural memory. Procedural memory is the agent's
skills and policies for how to do the work. In most systems much of it is not
a separate store: it lives in the system prompt, the tool definitions and the
code, and it changes when you deploy. Guidance the agent updates from its own
experience — a file of "lessons learned" it edits and reads back at every
start — needs its own write and review policy. Treat that as the most
sensitive write path in this chapter, because a bad entry there can change
many later runs, not one answer.

**What we will look at.** First where each kind of memory should live, and why
the embed-everything default does not suit semantic memory. Then what gets
written and who decides: there is a write policy even when nobody chose one.
Then a small test of what happens when the store holds two facts that
disagree. Then forgetting, which has to be designed in from the start. Then three practical
questions: whether memory is a tool the agent calls or infrastructure it never
sees, what survives a crash, and how you test a memory at all. And finally what
a system owes the people it remembers, all of which turns out to be schema
decisions rather than policy documents.

## Storage: stop reaching for a vector database first {#sec-memory-storage}

Three kinds of memory means three storage questions, and only one of them is
hard. Working memory lives in the context window because that is what a
context window is. Episodic memory is a log, and a log is a solved problem.
The interesting one is semantic memory, where the default instinct is to embed
everything and retrieve by similarity.

It is the wrong default, and the reason is the same one
@sec-context-engineering gave for structured data: **retrieval by similarity
score alone cannot express the operations memory actually needs.**

The operations are: *get this user's current preference*, *update it*,
*delete everything about this person*, *list what changed since March*. Those
are lookups and mutations on keys; none of them is a nearest-neighbour query.
They need fact identity, metadata, and update and delete rules; a vector index
can be an extra retrieval path on top of those.

| store | what it is genuinely good for | where it fails as memory |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Relational** | preferences, entities, anything with an identity you can key on; updates and deletes that actually delete | needs a schema and operating cost, so it cannot absorb whatever the model decides to remember |
| **Vector** | episodic recall — *have we discussed something like this before* | [cannot pick a *fact's* current value without fact identity and a validity policy]{.con}; two contradicting memories both retrieve happily, ranked by similarity rather than truth |
| **Graph** | relationships between entities, multi-hop questions about them | modelling and maintenance can be costly, and many projects never ask a question that needs it |
| **Key–value / document** | a small structured profile per user, read whole | querying across users or several fields may need extra indexes |

: Four stores, and what each is actually for {tbl-colwidths="[16,42,42]"}

The architecture that works for most systems is unglamorous and hybrid:

```text
  semantic memory   →  a table.   user_id, key, value, source, written_at
  episodic memory   →  a log, embedded for retrieval, with pointers back
                       to the full record
```

[Facts go in rows; episodes go in vectors.]{.hl}

A common design mistake in this area is putting facts in vectors without giving
them an identity. Not because the storage layer refuses: `pgvector` rows take ordinary
SQL `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and upsert (update the row if the key exists, insert it
otherwise), and every managed vector store has an id-keyed delete. The problem
is an append-only collection with no stable key for the fact.

If nothing enforces one row per `(user_id, key)` — say, one `preferred_channel`
per user — a corrected preference becomes a second embedding sitting next to
the first. Both are retrievable, and similarity search has no reason to prefer
the new one. Both update and delete turn out to be requirements rather than
nice-to-haves — one for correctness and, often, one for data-protection law —
and what both rest on is fact identity enforced in the schema. A unique constraint on
`(user_id, key)` works just as well on a `pgvector` table that also stores the
embedding. The point is the key, not where the vector lives; any similarity
index is a derived view over it. The unique constraint stops two active values
sitting on one key; on its own it does not satisfy a deletion request. That
also needs the copies in the index, the history table, caches and backups to
be handled according to the retention policy (@sec-memory-privacy).

## Write policies: the decision nobody makes on purpose {#sec-memory-write}

The previous section was about where a fact goes once you have decided to keep
it. This one is about that decision, which is the one nobody writes down.

What gets remembered is a policy, and if you do not choose one you have chosen
"whatever the model decides", which is a policy with known failure modes.

| who decides | how it behaves | when to use it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Rule-based** | you write the extractor: these fields, from these events | [predictable and auditable]{.pro}; a good default for fields that need auditing |
| **Model-decided** | the agent calls a `remember` tool when it judges something durable | flexible, and it will remember things you would not have — including things it should not |
| **User-confirmed** | the system proposes, the person approves | [increases the user's control]{.pro}; but a person can also approve a wrong or vague entry, and that approval is not legal consent on its own — an accuracy check and a proper legal basis are still needed; costs an interaction each time |

: Three write policies {tbl-colwidths="[20,44,36]"}

There is a second axis the table does not have, and it decides your security
posture rather than your precision: **what can reach this write path**.
Rule-based writes only what you named. User-confirmed writes only what a person
approved. Model-decided writes anything the model read — including tool output
and any document it was handed.

Four rules that hold up in production:

**Remember decisions and preferences, not conversation.** *The user prefers
invoices at the Levent office* is a fact with a shelf life. The paragraph in
which they said it is an episode, and belongs in the log rather than the
profile.

**Record provenance with every write.** When it was written, what event caused
it, and how confident the extractor was. Without provenance you cannot resolve
conflicts, cannot expire anything, and cannot answer *why does the system
think this about me* — which is a question you will be asked.

**Do not make an *inferred* preference durable without evidence.** A preference
you inferred once and a preference stated three times are different things. A
cheap useful policy separates the source: do not write anything inferred from
behaviour without evidence proportionate to its accuracy and privacy risk (a
second occurrence, say) or the user's confirmation — the same wrong inference
can recur. You can write an explicit durable statement the first time the user
makes it — they told you — but weigh that too for purpose, retention period and
the user's control.

**Never write attacker-controlled text as a fact.** This is the rule the other
three do not imply, and it is the one that makes memory qualitatively worse
than a bad prompt rather than the same problem again. A `remember` tool the
model can call *after reading a web page, a document, or a support ticket* is a
write path an attacker reaches without an account on your system: they put the
sentence in the content, the model judges it durable, and it survives every
later session. A one-shot injection becomes a permanent one, which is the
sentence @sec-agent-security picks this chapter up on. The mitigation is the
provenance field you already have: record the `source`, and do not carry
instructions found in retrieved documents or tool output into memory as a
user's statement or a system rule. If a fact from an external source is worth
keeping, store its source, trust level and validity period in their own fields,
and verify it or ask for confirmation before writing it as the user's
preference. And never let a recalled memory carry instructions into a system
prompt.

::: {.column-margin}
The failure mode of remembering everything is not storage cost — storage is
cheap. It is that the *retrieval* gets worse: every irrelevant memory is
another candidate competing with the relevant one, and @sec-retrieval's
measurements apply directly. A memory system that remembers everything is a
retrieval system with a deliberately degraded index.
:::

## Contradiction, measured {#sec-memory-conflict}

A store that accumulates facts will eventually hold two that disagree. The
design question is whether you have to *handle* that, or whether the model
sorts it out when it reads both.

It is a cheap question to answer, so here is the answer. Thirty invented
contradictions — the user preferred email in March and phone in July — under
three conditions with identical facts. Scored on whether the answer matches
the **newer** value. Half the items list the newer fact first, so position is
separated from recency.

**Scoring.** Every answer goes in exactly one of three buckets, so the columns
sum to 100% of the thirty items: *newer* if it names the July value and only
that, *older* if it names the March value and only that, *hedged* if it names
both, neither, or refuses. The 0.0% in the bare row is 0 of 30, not a rounded
small number. Read that row as an information control rather than a test of
temporal reasoning: with no dates and no rule, nothing in the context says which
fact is newer, so the row's "newer" column is not an accuracy measure but a sign
of whether the model picks one value under uncertainty. Hedging — 83.3% here —
is the defensible answer, and a careful model picks
neither value. Choosing the newer one 0 of 30 times fits that; choosing the
older one 5 of 30 times does not (see below).

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 30 contradictions per condition, n = 30
paired: the same thirty items run through all three conditions

 condition     chose newer   95% CI        hedged   newer listed first / last
 bare            0/30  0.0%   [ 0.0, 11.4]   83.3%          0.0%  /   0.0%
 dated          10/30 33.3%   [19.2, 51.2]   66.7%         33.3%  /  33.3%
 dated+rule     25/30 83.3%   [66.4, 92.7]   16.7%         66.7%  / 100.0%
```

Three things, in order of how much they should change what you build.

**In this measurement, timestamps alone were not enough.** Adding *[recorded 12 March 2025]* and
*[recorded 28 July 2025]* moved the model from never choosing the newer fact
to choosing it a third of the time. Two-thirds of the time it still declined
to choose. If your memory design is "store the date and let the model work it
out", this small measurement says that is unreliable at least for this setup;
measure it yourself on another model.

**An explicit rule does most of the work, and not all of it.** Adding one
sentence — *when facts conflict, use the most recently recorded one* — took it
to 83.3%. That is a large, cheap improvement. Still, one answer in six hedges
instead of naming the newer value, though none picks the older one.

The three intervals in the table do not overlap, but comparing intervals is not
the right test here either: the three conditions ran on the *same* thirty
items, so the comparison between them is paired. Nothing was correct in `bare`, so the bare-to-dated
step has ten discordant pairs all in one direction: McNemar's exact test gives
p = 0.002. The dated-to-rule step adds fifteen net, and across every split of
the discordant pairs consistent with those margins the exact p runs from
6 × 10⁻⁵ to 0.004. The Wilson intervals in the table size each proportion;
they are not the test of the difference.

**The rule interacts with position, and that is the least comfortable number
here.** In the `dated+rule` condition the model was right on 15 of 15 items
where the newer fact was listed *last*, and on 10 of 15 where it was listed
*first* — 100% against 66.7%, two-sided Fisher exact p = 0.042. That is
fifteen items per cell and a split chosen after looking, so treat it as a
exploratory warning worth checking on your own model rather than a law. In
`bare` and `dated` no difference was observed (0.0/0.0 and 33.3/33.3), but
that does not prove there is no position effect there; in this sample it
showed up only once the rule was present. Read conservatively:
with the rule, accuracy is somewhere between two thirds and 100%, depending on
an ordering you did not think you were choosing. Which is one more argument for
the conclusion below: resolve in retrieval, inject one fact, and there is no
ordering left to get wrong.

[Conflict resolution belongs in your retrieval code, not in your prompt.]{.hl}
Resolve before you inject: return one fact, the one your policy chose, and the
model has nothing to be inconsistent about. That is a good default for
*current-value* questions; for questions about history, or ones that are
genuinely ambiguous, keep the versions and the reason for the resolution, and
do not silently hide the conflict. Published systems moved the same
decision out of the answering prompt, in two different ways.
@rasmussen2025zep builds the store on a bi-temporal graph — each fact carries
both when it was true and when the system learned it — and, when a new fact
contradicts an old one, *invalidates* the superseded edge by recording when it
stopped being true, rather than keeping two live facts side by side.
@chhikara2025mem0 resolves conflicts at write time: for each new fact, an LLM
call compares it with similar stored memories and chooses to add, update,
delete or do nothing. A model still decides there, but once, on one pair, when
the fact is written — not every time a question is answered. This measurement
is a small local argument for an architecture other people arrived at from the
other direction.

**This model's default behaviour was hedging, not lying.** In the bare condition the
model picked the *older* fact 16.7% of the time and gave both or neither
**83.3%** of the time. That is better than confidently picking wrong — but a
system that answers "your preference is email, or possibly phone" has failed
the user just as thoroughly, and it fails in a form that is harder to detect
than a wrong answer. In the bare condition the hedge is the model's most
honest reply; the failure belongs to the system, which gave it no way to
decide.

The grey band shows answers that pick no single value. In the conditions with
dates and a rule it is a failure people often do not plan for: not a wrong
answer but no answer, and it shrinks rather than disappears as you add
machinery to the prompt. In the undated control condition, stating the
uncertainty is the appropriate reply. Note also that the older fact is chosen only in the bare
condition (5 of 30), and never once dates are added. Without dates the model
cannot know which fact is older; that all five picks landed on the older value
may be chance (two-sided exact binomial p ≈ 0.06) or an artefact of how the
items were built, and this probe cannot tell which.
:::

::::

::: {.column-margin}
Small measurement, narrow claim: one model, thirty items, intervals up to 32
points wide. What it establishes is the *ordering* — bare < dated < dated+rule —
and the practical conclusion, which does not depend on the exact figures: do
not leave contradiction resolution to the model when a `WHERE` clause and an
`ORDER BY … LIMIT 1` over your precedence columns will do it exactly.
:::

### So what should the retrieval side do?

Resolve, then inject. Concretely, four rules for most cases:

- **One active fact per key, for a single-valued field.** If the store can hold
  two active values for *preferred channel*, the ambiguity reaches the model.
  If a field can legitimately hold several values at once (several phone
  numbers, say), widen the key accordingly. Make the write path an upsert and
  the ambiguity never exists. An upsert overwrites, though, and *list what
  changed since March* needs the old value: copy it to a history table (or to
  the episode log) before overwriting, or keep every version as a row with
  `valid_from` and `valid_to` and read only the open one — the same idea as
  the bi-temporal store above. The upsert is also the moment to check
  precedence: if the new value comes from a weaker source than the stored one,
  keep the stored one and log the conflict.
- **Recency wins by default**, because it is usually right and it is the rule
  users expect. Recency of *what*, though: record
  the time the fact was true and the time you learned it separately, because a
  late-arriving report of an old event is not news. Where recency is wrong — a
  stated preference should outrank an inferred one regardless of date, and an
  authoritative source should outrank a guess — encode *that*, explicitly, as a
  precedence over source and event time rather than over write time.
- **Expire on a schedule, not on faith.** Anything time-sensitive gets a TTL
  (*time to live*: how long the fact counts as valid) or a review date at write
  time. A shipping address ages slowly (periodic confirmation may do instead of
  a TTL); a *current project* ages fast. A TTL is a freshness tool, not a
  measure of truth: an unexpired address can change, and expired information
  can still be right. For critical fields, re-verify on expiry rather than
  deleting or using the value blindly; for a shipping address that may mean
  asking the user.
- **Surface conflicts you cannot resolve.** If two sources of equal precedence
  disagree, the honest move is to ask, not to guess — and it is a much better
  user experience than either answer.

## Forgetting is a feature {#sec-memory-forgetting}

Systems that only accumulate get worse, and the degradation is not obvious
because nothing errors. Three mechanisms, all cheap to add at the start and
awkward to retrofit:

- **TTL at write time.** Set a retention and re-verification period for each
  kind of memory; every fact carries an expiry or a recorded, justified
  exemption, and an expired record drops out of active retrieval. The decision
  is easy when you are writing the extractor and very hard six months later.
- **Decay for episodes.** Rank retrieval by relevance *and* age. An episode
  from last week is usually more useful than an identical one from last year,
  and a pure similarity ranking cannot express that.
- **Deletion that deletes.** Not a `deleted` flag that the retriever forgets
  to filter on. This is @sec-governance's requirement and it is a good reason
  on its own to keep facts in a store where `DELETE` means what it says. But
  `DELETE` alone is not enough: a deletion request needs its own erase or
  make-inaccessible steps for the main store, derived indexes, caches, logs and
  backups.

## A tool the agent calls, or infrastructure it never sees? {#sec-memory-interface}

Everything so far has been about the store. This section is about the wire
between the store and the agent, and there are two basic ways to run it — most
systems combine them for reads and writes — which trade the same thing @sec-agent-anatomy's levels of autonomy traded: capability
against predictability.

**Memory as a tool.** The agent gets `remember(fact)` and `recall(query)` and
decides when to use them. It is visible in the transcript, so you can audit
what was written and why, and the agent can choose not to bother. The cost is
that it is another decision the model can get wrong. On its own task,
@sec-tool-design measured a tool with an opaque schema going uncalled on 41.7%
of tasks (25/60); but that rate belongs to a different task and tool
definition, not an expected rate for memory tools. Measure this risk on your
own tasks, as the memory tool's call rate and correct-recall success.

**Memory as infrastructure.** Before every run, your code retrieves what is
relevant and injects it into the context — typically a clearly delimited block
labelled as stored data about the user, not as instructions, which is the
write-path rule above applied on the read side. The agent never knows there is
a memory system; it simply knows things. This is predictable and testable;
keyed retrieval may need no model decision at all, while semantic selection
(similarity ranking, reranking) is a separate retrieval and security decision
— and it is the right default for the same reason a
fixed pipeline is the right default in @sec-agent-anatomy.

The combination most production systems land on: **read as infrastructure,
write as a tool.** Recall happens automatically because it should happen every
time; writing is an explicit act, because it is the one you want in the log.
"Write as a tool" does not mean handing the write path to the model: the tool
is an explicit, logged act that goes through the write-policy rules above,
refuses writes whose `source` is retrieved content, and asks the user to
confirm where needed. The tool is where the rules are enforced, not a
replacement for them.

## Sessions, checkpoints, and resume {#sec-memory-sessions}

A long-running agent will be interrupted — a deploy, a timeout, a crash, a
user closing the tab. What survives that is a design decision, and the useful
framing is that **the transcript is a value you can persist**, not a thing
that lives in a process.

- **Checkpoint step by step**, not at the end. Choose the frequency from your
  loss tolerance and cost; for long agents that usually means after every
  step. The unit is one loop iteration: the messages so far, plus whatever your
  runtime needs to continue.
- **Store the tool results, not just the calls.** Replaying a run by
  re-executing its tools is wrong for anything that writes, and slow for
  everything else.
- **Guard side-effecting tools against running twice.** The tool action and the
  checkpoint are not atomic: a crash between them can make a resumed run repeat
  the same write. Give side-effecting calls a call id, make the tool idempotent
  (a second call with the same id changes nothing), and test that crash window
  on its own.
- **Make resume the same code path as start.** A resumed run that takes a
  different branch is a second implementation you will not test.

@packer2023memgpt is the reference design for taking this seriously — an agent
that manages its own *paging*, the operating-system term for moving data
between a small fast memory and a large slow one: here, between the context
window and external storage. It is a good starting point for examining the
operating-system paging analogy in detail.

## Evaluating a memory {#sec-memory-eval}

A memory can fail at three points, and each needs its own check.

- **The write.** Of the facts the system stored, how many should it have
  stored (precision)? Of the facts it should have stored, how many did it
  store (recall)? For a first evaluation, a labelled set of a few dozen
  conversations, each with the facts a careful person would keep, is enough.
  A production decision needs a broader set covering different users, topics
  and kinds of sensitive data; a small set does not measure rare privacy
  violations reliably. Count forbidden writes
  — injected instructions, data you promised not to keep — separately, because
  one of those matters more than ten missed preferences.
- **The read.** For current-preference questions, does recall return the
  *current* value and apply source precedence correctly; for questions about
  history, does it fetch the relevant versions? The contradiction probe above is
  a test of this kind, and so are steps 3 and 4 of the lab. For both kinds,
  test separately that another user's memory never comes back for any query,
  that unauthorised access is refused, that the system abstains when nothing was
  stored, and that deleted information does not return.
- **The whole loop, over many sessions.** Public benchmarks do this with long
  multi-session conversations and questions about them:
  [LoCoMo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17753) (Maharana et al., 2024) and
  [LongMemEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10813) (Wu et al., 2024), whose
  question types include *knowledge updates* — this chapter's contradiction
  problem — and *abstention*, answering "I don't know" when nothing was stored.
  @chhikara2025mem0 reports on LoCoMo and @rasmussen2025zep on LongMemEval.
  Numbers from different papers are rarely comparable: the answering model, the
  judge and the prompt all differ.

The general machinery — judges, confidence intervals, paired comparisons — is
@sec-agent-eval's subject; what is specific to memory is that the questions
have to be asked *after* time has passed and facts have changed.

## Privacy, consent, and deletion {#sec-memory-privacy}

A system that remembers people has obligations that a stateless one does not,
and the engineering decisions that satisfy them are made in
@sec-memory-storage rather than in a policy document written afterwards.

**Deletion has to actually delete.** This is the concrete reason facts belong
in a store with a real `DELETE`. The right is written into law: the GDPR's
right to erasure (Article 17) in the EU, and in Türkiye KVKK Article 7, which
requires personal data to be deleted, destroyed or anonymised once the reason
for processing it is gone, with Article 11 giving the person the right to ask;
@sec-governance-kvkk covers both regimes. These obligations have exceptions and
retention duties, and a single SQL `DELETE` does not make you compliant. What
the technical design can do is make it possible to find, and where required
destroy, the traces in indexes, caches, backups and derived copies along with
the main record; the legal assessment has to be made separately. Erasing *a
whole user* is the easy case if every vector carries a `user_id`. "We embed
everything" becomes a
problem the first time someone asks you to forget or correct *one specific
thing*: a vector index deletes a vector by id, not a fact. Unless you kept a
mapping from each fact to the vectors that encode it, you first have to find
them. Searching an index for every trace of one fact to honour one request is
the cost of the architecture decision, paid later.

**Provenance is what makes an answer possible.** *Why does this system think I
prefer phone calls?* is a question with a good answer only if you recorded
which event caused the write. It is one column, added at the start.

**Inference is not consent.** A preference the user stated is different from
one your extractor inferred, and users experience the second as surveillance
even when it is accurate. Store the distinction, use it in precedence rules —
and when a memory drives something visible, be able to show what it was based
on. Allow for the extractor producing health, religion, political views or
anything else the law treats as special-category data *by inference* (GDPR
Article 9, KVKK Article 6): an accurate guess about such a thing can itself
count as sensitive processing. If your product policy forbids such inferences —
the safe default for most memory systems — block them in the extractor; if
processing is intended, assess the applicable legal conditions and extra
safeguards separately. And "consent" in this chapter means the everyday sense — the person
saw the memory and agreed. Whether that is also your legal basis under KVKK or
the GDPR is a separate question; @sec-governance-kvkk explains why consent is
rarely the basis that fits.

**Every read is filtered by user.** A serious incident class specific to memory
systems is one user's memory entering another user's context, usually because
a query forgot its `user_id` filter. Enforce the filter in the access layer
rather than adding it to each query by hand (row-level security in
PostgreSQL, for example), and keep a test that searches for another user's
data and must come back empty.

**Retention is a decision, not a default.** Everything written gets an expiry
or an explicit exemption. @sec-governance is where this becomes a regime; the
part that belongs here is that an expiry column is easy to add at write time
and very hard to backfill convincingly afterwards. Choosing the periods,
applying them and auditing deletion still take design and operational work
either way.

::: {.column-margin}
The uncomfortable version of this section: most memory systems are built by
adding writes until the demos improve, and the privacy work is done at the end
by someone else. Almost every requirement above is a *schema* decision —
provenance, source, expiry, deletability — which means it is cheap on day one
and expensive on day two hundred.
:::

## Intuition checks {#sec-memory-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. One is settled by the measurement this
chapter runs; the other five are design decisions it argues for, and most of
them come down to a schema choice that costs nothing on day one.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Should memory go in a vector database?

Episodes, usually yes; current facts, not on their own. Similarity search is
right for *have we discussed something like this* and the wrong tool for *what
is this user's current preference*.
Be precise about why, because "you cannot delete from a vector store" is not
it — you can, by id. What a vector index does not give you is a *key*: nothing
stops two contradictory embeddings of the same preference coexisting, and
nearest-neighbour search has no notion of which is current. Facts go in rows
keyed by `(user, key)`, where an upsert makes two active values on one key
impossible; those rows can live in a relational table or in a table that also
has a vector column — what matters is telling the old and new versions of the
same preference apart. Episodes go in an index with pointers back to the
record. Putting facts in
vectors without a key is a common production mistake in this area, and you pay
for it the first time a user asks you to correct or forget one specific fact.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Two memories contradict. Will the model sort it out?

Not reliably, in this test. In the undated control condition the model picked
no single value in 83.3% of answers; with no chronology visible, that is the
expected uncertain answer. Adding timestamps raised the rate of choosing the
newer value to 33.3%. Adding an explicit "prefer the most recent" rule
got it to 83.3% — better, and still one answer in six hedging. One model and
thirty items do not generalise, but the ordering is clear: for current-value
questions, resolve in the retrieval layer and inject one fact.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
Note which direction the failure goes: hedging, not confident error. That is
the better failure, but a system that answers "email, or possibly phone" has
still failed. A bare accuracy number does not show whether a miss was a hedge
or a wrong pick.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. What should trigger a write to memory?

Not a single *inference*. The cheapest policy that works separates the two
cases: an explicit durable statement — *always email me, never call* — can be
written the first time, because the user said it; anything you inferred needs a
second occurrence or a confirmation. And
record provenance with every write, because without it you cannot resolve
conflicts, expire anything, or answer why the system believes something. The
failure mode of remembering everything is not storage cost but retrieval
quality: every irrelevant memory competes with the relevant one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Which memory type fails most dangerously?

Usually semantic. Working memory can fail loudly when you hit the window, but
it can also quietly miss information inside a long context. Episodic memory
fails slowly — retrieval gets worse and costs rise. Semantic memory fails
**silently**: a fact recorded in March is returned confidently in July, with
nothing in the system aware it expired. That asymmetry is why TTLs belong at
write time rather than on a cleanup backlog.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Should the agent decide what to remember?

Only where a wrong write is cheap. Model-decided writes are flexible and will
remember things you would not have chosen, including things you are not
allowed to keep. Rule-based extraction is predictable and auditable, a good
default for fields that need auditing; user-confirmed writes cost an
interaction and increase the user's control, but the legal basis, notice and
retention terms still have to be assessed separately. Choose the write path by
risk and data type. Most systems
want read-as-infrastructure and write-as-an-explicit-act.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your agent crashed mid-run. What should survive?

The transcript, checkpointed after every step rather than at the end, with
tool *results* and call ids stored durably, not just the calls — replaying a
run by re-executing its tools is wrong for anything that writes, and storing
results alone does not stop a double execution after a crash between the tool
and the checkpoint. Make side-effecting calls idempotent, or look up the
previous result before retrying, and test that race. And resume should be the same code
path as start, because a separate resume path is a second implementation that
will not get tested.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-memory-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** Some of these are
adapted from topics in the two open interview sources introduced there (Chip
Huyen's *Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews* book and the *Machine
Learning Interviews* repository), and some are written around this chapter's
design discussion and local contradiction test; none is attributed to a
particular company, and the numbers in the answers are this chapter's own.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the design

**Q: How would you design memory for a conversational agent?**

Start by splitting the word: working memory is the transcript and belongs to
context engineering; episodic memory is an event log, retrieved by similarity;
semantic memory is facts, and belongs in rows keyed by user and attribute with
provenance and an expiry. Then say what each store must support — facts need
update and delete, episodes need ranking by relevance and age — and note that
this is why "embed everything" falls short: without a stable identity and a
versioning policy per fact, nothing guarantees a single current value. A
similarity index can be a retrieval path to those records, not a replacement
for them.

**Q: Two memories contradict. What happens?**

Resolve before injection, in code, and give the model one fact. If you leave it
to the model, expect inconsistency: measured on a small probe, timestamps alone
produced the newer answer a third of the time, and even with an explicit recency
rule one answer in six still hedged. The interesting follow-up is
where recency is the *wrong* rule — a stated preference should outrank an
inferred one whatever the dates — which is why precedence is over source as
well as time.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: A user asks you to delete everything you know about them. What happens?**

Walk the actual data path: the fact store, the vector index, the episode log,
summaries, logs, backups, any cache, and external providers if there are any.
The honest answer names the hard one. Deleting *a user* is comparatively easy —
every store can delete by id — though derived summaries, external providers
and backups complicate even that; verify each layer's deletion or destruction
process and its retention exceptions separately. Deleting *a fact* is
where an embedding-only design hurts: you have to know which vectors encode it,
which means you needed the mapping from fact to embedding all along, and
derived copies inside summaries are harder still. Say that this is a schema decision
made on day one, not a feature added later, and that it is the strongest
practical argument for keeping facts in a relational store.

**Q: Your agent keeps acting on outdated information. Where do you look?**

At the write and read paths together. Ask whether anything carried a TTL,
whether writes upsert or append, and about versioning and source precedence;
on the read side look at the query filter, ranking and caches, and check
whether retrieval returns one fact per key or several. A common "stale memory"
bug is really a "two active values for one key" bug, and its fix is a unique
constraint rather than a smarter prompt.

## Lab: build a memory that can be wrong safely {#sec-memory-lab}

Six steps, and the first one has no code in it on purpose — a memory system
you cannot describe in a paragraph is one whose write policy you have not
chosen.

### Step 1 — write the policy before the code

Three things your system must remember, three it must never store, and for
each of the three it stores: who decides, and when does it expire.

### Step 2 — a table, not an index

`user_id, key, value, source, valid_from, written_at, expires_at` — with
`valid_from` for when the fact became true and `written_at` for when you
learned it. Upsert on `(user_id, key)` so two values for one key cannot exist,
and copy the old value to a history table before you overwrite it.

### Step 3 — plant a contradiction

Write a preference, then write a different one. Query it. If your retrieval
returns both, fix the retrieval — this chapter measured what happens when the
model is left to resolve it.

### Step 4 — measure staleness

Simulate six months passing: on a copy of your store, move every timestamp
back six months, then ask ten questions. Shifting dates does not change the
answers, so judge each one yourself — would this fact probably still be true
after six months (an address, yes; a current project, often not)? Count the
answers that are probably wrong now. That number is what a TTL is worth, and
the keys behind them are the ones that need one.

### Step 5 — delete a user, then look

Run your deletion path, then search the raw store, the index, the logs, and
any cache for the person's data. Report where it survived.

### Step 6 — answer "why do you think that?"

For three memories, produce the event that caused each write. If you cannot,
add the provenance column now.

### What to hand in

The policy from step 1, the staleness count from step 4, the list of places
data survived deletion in step 5, and one sentence naming the memory your
system should stop writing.

## Exercises {#sec-memory-exercises}

1. **The write policy.** For a support agent: three things it must remember,
   three it must never store, and for each stored item who decides and when it
   expires. One page, before any code.
2. **Plant a contradiction.** Put two conflicting facts in your store, then
   decide the resolution rule and defend it against the case where recency is
   the wrong answer.
3. **Age your store.** Move every timestamp back six months and re-ask ten
   questions. For each answer, judge whether the fact behind it would probably
   still be true six months later; count the ones that would not. That is what
   you are buying with a TTL.
4. **Delete and hunt.** Run your deletion path for one user, then search every
   store, index, log and cache. Write down where the data survived.
5. **Provenance audit.** Pick five memories and produce the event that caused
   each. If you cannot for any of them, that is the finding.
6. **Facts versus episodes.** Take your current memory store and classify every
   entry as one or the other. If facts are in the vector index, estimate what
   moving them costs now against what it costs in a year.
7. **Tool or infrastructure.** Implement recall both ways on the same task and
   compare: how often does the agent forget to call the tool, and what does
   automatic injection cost you in tokens?

## Where to go deeper {#sec-memory-deeper}

Before reading: take your memory store and classify ten entries as fact or
episode. If facts are living in a vector index, you have found your first task.

| resource | what it is |

| [`letta`](https://github.com/letta-ai/letta) | the MemGPT design as a working system — the clearest way to see self-managed paging between context and storage |
| [`mem0`](https://github.com/mem0ai/mem0) | a memory layer with explicit extraction and update policies; useful to read for the policy vocabulary even if you build your own |
| [`graphiti`](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti) | Zep's open-source temporal knowledge graph: facts with validity intervals, which is the contradiction problem taken seriously |
| [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic | the surrounding argument for why less machinery usually wins |
| [Lil'Log on agents](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/) | the widely read survey post that maps the human-memory vocabulary (short-term, long-term; episodic, semantic, procedural) onto agent components — note that it maps all long-term memory onto a vector store, the default this chapter argues against |
| [CoALA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02427) — Sumers et al. | the paper behind the working / episodic / semantic / procedural taxonomy for language agents |

## What to remember {#sec-memory-summary}

- **Three memories, three failure modes.** Working memory fails loudly when the
  window fills; episodic memory fails slowly as volume degrades retrieval;
  **semantic memory fails silently**, returning a March fact confidently in
  July.
- **Facts in rows, episodes in vectors.** A fact needs update and delete, and a
  vector index offers them only by vector id, not by fact. Putting facts in an
  index without a key is a common production mistake, and you pay for it the
  first time a user asks you to correct or forget one specific fact.
- **The model will not resolve contradictions for you.** With both facts
  present and no timestamps it chose the newer one **0%** of the time and
  hedged on 83.3%; timestamps alone took it to 33.3%; an explicit recency rule
  took it to 83.3% and left one answer in six hedging. Resolve in retrieval,
  inject one fact.
- **Hedging is the default failure.** Not a confident wrong answer but "email,
  or possibly phone" — better than lying, still a failed answer, and a bare
  accuracy number cannot tell it apart from a wrong pick.
- **Write an explicit statement the first time, and an inference only on a
  second occurrence or a confirmation**, and record provenance every time.
  Without provenance you cannot resolve, expire, or explain.
- **Test the write, the read and the whole loop.** Write precision and
  recall, "does recall return the current value", and questions asked after
  facts have changed.
- **Forgetting is a feature.** TTL at write time, decay for episodes, and
  deletion that actually deletes rather than a flag the retriever might forget.
- **Read as infrastructure, write as a tool.** Recall should happen every time
  and needs no model decision; writing is the act you want visible in the
  transcript.
- **Privacy requirements are schema decisions.** Provenance, source, expiry and
  deletability cost nothing on day one and are close to impossible to add
  convincingly on day two hundred.
